title: A Single Neuron Is Sufficient to Bypass Safety Alignment in Large Language Models
claim: A single neuron's activation sharply separates harmful from harmless inputs token by token, and alignment training changes its polarity and strength.
layout: 2 stacked rounded boxes, harmful vs harmless columns, token-level heatmap highlights
description: Two rounded boxes hold real prompt text with per-token activation highlighting. The top box has a red 'Harmful' column on the left and a green 'Harmless' column on the right. It has two model rows: Qwen3-32B (layer 40, neuron F15515) and Llama-3.1-8B (layer 11, neuron F4258). In the harmful column, tokens such as 'meth', 'amphetamine', '?', 'murder' and the chat-template tokens are shaded in saturated red. The harmless prompts ('What is the capital of France?', 'a murder of crows') are mostly unshaded, with faint pink on 'murder'. The bottom box compares Qwen3-8B (layer 14, neuron F7924) Instruct on the left with Base on the right, on the same bomb-making prompt. Tokens are shaded in blue, which marks negative activation. The eye goes first to the red-highlighted harmful prompts at top left.
caption: Per-token activations of refusal neurons. Top: Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-8B on harmful and harmless prompts; the neuron fires \textcolor[rgb]{0.882,0.341,0.349}{positively} on harmful prompts. (More results: Fig. [ref]). Bottom: Qwen3-8B instruct vs.\ base on the same harmful prompt; the neuron fires \textcolor[rgb]{0.478,0.608,0.710}{negatively} on harmful prompts. (More results: Fig. [ref])
abstract: Safety alignment in language models operates through two mechanistically distinct systems: refusal neurons that gate whether harmful knowledge is expressed, and concept neurons that encode the harmful knowledge itself. By targeting a single neuron in each system, we demonstrate both directions of failure -- bypassing safety on explicit harmful requests via suppression, and inducing harmful content from innocent prompts via amplification -- across seven models spanning two families and 1.7B to 70B parameters, without any training or prompt engineering. Our findings suggest that safety alignment is not robustly distributed across model weights but is mediated by individual neurons that are each causally sufficient to gate refusal behavior -- suppressing any one of the identified refusal neurons bypasses safety alignment across diverse harmful requests.
